extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics and mathematicians interested in 19th-century foundations/rigor (graduate students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical-analysis of Abel's comment that Cauchy's theorem 'admitted exceptions', situating that remark in early-19th-century debates about rigor, convergence, and the transition from formula-centered to concept-centered analysis. Traces Abel's examples, proofs, and replies (exception-barring, critical revision) and the wider methodological implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of convergence and determination of the sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish convergence of a series as a process distinct from finding its sum; Abel insisted on a 'complete separation of the two processes of finding a sum: (a) convergence of the series and (b) determination of the sum of the series.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abel used this separation as a methodological principle when criticizing Cauchy and when extending proofs (e.g., the binomial theorem to complex exponents). Anti-pattern: inserting numerical values or treating sum-evaluation and convergence as a single step can produce 'false sums' (Poisson Paradox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing from the special to the general (no unjustified generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not generalize from special cases to universal theorems without rigorous justification; Cauchy criticized the 'generality of algebra' and Abel warned that reasoning 'from the special to the general' leads to paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing proofs or theorems, make explicit the assumptions and avoid relying on formal algebraic manipulations that hold only in special contexts. Historical anti-pattern: trusting formal equality of expressions without numerical checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of limit processes / uniformity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof implicitly uses two limit processes (e.g., n → ∞ and α → 0), these processes must be handled so their interrelation is controlled (modern condition: uniform convergence or an explicit uniformity hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy's argument for continuity of a sum of continuous functions fails because the limits are not independent. Abel's and later authors' corrections introduce uniform convergence concepts. Anti-pattern: treating tails/remainders as vanishing uniformly without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware insertion of numerical values into formal equalities (Poisson Paradox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not naively substitute numerical values into an algebraic/formal equality between a series and a closed expression; Poisson's example showed a convergent series may evaluate to a different value than the formal closed form for particular substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test formal equalities under substitution and check domain of validity. Use as a diagnostic: if substitution yields contradictions (e.g., 0+0+0+... = π/2), the formal equality's domain needs clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring / restricting the theorem to a subclass
rubrics_metrics.description: When a general theorem 'admits exceptions,' one acceptable response is to restrict the theorem to a subclass of objects where the problematic behavior does not occur (Lakatos' 'exception-barring'). Abel replaced Theorem C by a narrower theorem (Theorem A1) tailored to series of a particular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic strategy preserves usable results (e.g., for the binomial theorem) but requires careful justification that the restricted class indeed avoids the identified problems. Anti-pattern: arbitrary restriction without structural justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counterexamples to delimit and refine theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions in the transitional period evolve into counterexamples in the concept-centered approach and are used to refute or refine theorems by showing precisely where hypotheses fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze series (e.g., trigonometric series) that violate a proposed statement to determine the necessary additional conditions. In later practice, counterexamples are central to 'critical revision' and theorem reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical revision of theory (restate and reframe results with precise conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate process of reworking previously accepted formulae/theorems into precisely stated, concept-centered theorems with explicit hypotheses and domain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historiographically and methodologically, apply critical revision by examining prior assumptions, making hidden uniformity or domain requirements explicit, and recasting statements so they 'no longer admit exceptions.' Abel's work is presented as an instance of this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check uniform boundedness of tails as functions of the variable
rubrics_metrics.description: When bounding the tail of a series by a quantity (p or θ(x)), ensure that the bound is uniform in the variable over the domain of interest; Abel tacitly treated θ(x) as a constant, hiding a uniformity requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly verify whether an m (index beyond which tails are small) can be chosen independent of x. Failure to do so can produce counterexamples to purported continuity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity at boundary points requires explicit conditions (e.g., Abel-type theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity or limit-equality statements at the boundary of convergence are not automatic; additional hypotheses (e.g., particular forms of coefficients, types of convergence) are required (Abel's Theorem A2/A1 concerns continuity when variable approaches boundary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting continuity up to boundary, supply precise hypotheses (absolute convergence, specific coefficient behavior, or uniformity conditions). Be aware Abel's original proofs were later shown to lack necessary uniformity and may be false as stated without extra conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-power (trigonometric) series as stress tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Trigonometric and other non-power series often expose false general conclusions valid only for power series; Abel recommended testing accepted statements using such series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theorem was established mainly using power series examples, attempt counterexamples from different classes (e.g., Fourier-type series) to test generality. Abel used series like sin(nx)/n to show discontinuities and limits of Theorem C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for power-series methods as 'safe' or aesthetically preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Power series were regarded as formally simpler and better behaved, and thus often used as a 'safe haven' when restricting general theorems (Abel valued power series for their aesthetic and structural properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While power-series techniques can avoid certain paradoxes, recognize this is partly aesthetic and pragmatic; ensure that reliance on power series is justified for the problem at hand rather than hiding unproven assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formula-centered vs concept-centered mathematical styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess mathematical work according to whether it is 'formula-centered' (emphasis on formal manipulations, tolerant of exceptions, appeals to intuition) or 'concept-centered' (emphasis on concepts, precise definitions, explicit hypotheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to interpret proofs, methods, and the tolerance for exceptions in historical works. The transition from formula- to concept-centered analysis explains differing reactions to exceptions and the later primacy of counterexamples and explicit conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace provenance and transmission of texts/examples when interpreting historical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributing remarks or examples (e.g., Abel's footnote), verify manuscript sources, translations (Crelle's German translation, Holmboe's edition), and possible editorial interventions; authorship and phrasing affect interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evaluation should examine manuscript survival, translations, editorial practices, and correspondence (letters to Holmboe, Hansteen) to understand whether phrasing (e.g., 'admit exceptions') is authorial or editorial, and how that affects methodological claims.
